Work on the building's foundation commenced in August 1970. Contractors excavated the lot to a depth of 50 feet (15 m), and they removed 180,000 cubic feet (5,100 m3) of dirt from the site.[[25]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-p169075911-25) By that November, Spencer, White & Prentis Inc. was excavating a trench around the site, measuring 60 feet (18 m) deep and 20 by 216 feet (6.1 by 65.8 m) across. The contractors then built a [slurry wall](Slurry_wall "Slurry wall") within the trench, made of concrete and reinforced steel.[[26]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n109124635-26) Workers used steel bracing to prevent the slurry wall from collapsing inward, then used [caissons](Caisson_(engineering) "Caisson (engineering)") to drill 201 holes into the ground. They also rerouted a sewer that had run underneath Quincy Street, which was to be closed permanent as part of the tower's construction.[[25]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-p169075911-25)

The Diesel Construction Company was hired as the Sears Tower's [general contractor](General_contractor "General contractor").[[27]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-p133809828-27) Sears, Roebuck & Co. chairman Gordon M. Metcalf installed the building's first steel beam at a ceremony on June 7, 1971.[[28]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n109125056-28)[[29]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-nyt-1971-06-08-29) The project employed 2,000 workers. To accelerate the building's construction, a concrete plant was built in the building's basement, allowing workers to pour one-third of a concrete floor every day. Contractors built two temporary kitchens on the site for workers, and telephone and loudspeaker systems were installed on every floor to allow workers to communicate. In addition, contractors installed temporary generators that could supply up to 14,000 kilowatts (19,000 hp) simultaneously; during the winter, most of this electricity was used to heat the exposed steel beams on the lowest five floors.[[30]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n109125194-30)

#### Broadcast-signal controversy

By late 1971, <Chicagoland> residents and broadcasters had raised concerns that the new Sears Tower would disrupt television broadcasts.[[31]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-p1014881361-31)[[32]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n109139976-32) According to one estimate, the building would obstruct television signals for 15 percent of Chicagoans and cause "double images" for another 20 percent,[[31]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-p1014881361-31) primarily affecting communities to the northwest and southeast.[[32]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n109139976-32) The same year, officials of the village of [Skokie](Skokie%2C_Illinois "Skokie, Illinois"), northwest of Chicago, threatened to request an injunction to prevent further construction.[[33]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-p1862362537-33)[[34]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-p169116946-34) In response to these concerns, Sears started researching methods to reduce the tower's effect on broadcast signals. *Variety* magazine stated that the Sears Tower did not interfere with broadcasts on its own, since several shorter towers in the Loop also interfered with broadcast signals.[[35]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-p962900933-35) Nonetheless, the Illinois Citizens' Committee for Broadcasting filed a formal complaint with the [Federal Communications Commission](Federal_Communications_Commission "Federal Communications Commission") (FCC) in February 1972.[[36]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-p962940770-36)[[37]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-37)

### 20th century

#### Opening and early years

The first Sears employees began moving into the tower during the weekend of September 9, 1973.[[71]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n109411769-71)[[75]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-p1627236636-75) Flashing [beacons](Beacon "Beacon") on the building's roof, the first to be installed at any building in Chicago, were activated the same month.[[76]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n109411685-76) Upon the tower's opening, broadcasters at the [John Hancock Center](John_Hancock_Center "John Hancock Center"), Chicago's second-tallest building, had to decide whether to relocate to the Sears Tower.[[77]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-p963306761-77) Two television stations decided to relocate.[[78]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n109412135-78) Six other stations remained at the John Hancock Center, citing a study which showed that relocating to the Sears Tower would provide only minimal benefits.[[78]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n109412135-78)[[79]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-p1032471721-79) Documents released in late 1973 indicated that the Sears Tower would cause much more interference than either Sears or the television stations had disclosed.[[79]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-p1032471721-79) WLS-TV moved to the Sears Tower in February 1974,[[80]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-p494041980-80) followed by WTTW the next month.[[81]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-81)

By March 1974, three-fourths of the space in the building was occupied; Sears had leased the upper stories to tenants such as [Goldman Sachs](Goldman_Sachs "Goldman Sachs"), [Northwest Industries](Northwest_Industries "Northwest Industries"), and [Schiff Hardin](Schiff_Hardin "Schiff Hardin").[[82]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n109413042-82) A [mobile](Mobile_(sculpture) "Mobile (sculpture)") sculpture by [Alexander Calder](Alexander_Calder "Alexander Calder") was dedicated in the lobby in October 1974.[[83]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n109412727-83)[[84]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-Drexler_Menges_2009_p.-84) Sears' optimistic growth projections were not realized; instead, in late 1974, the company fired 500 workers, about seven percent of the 7,000 Sears employees that worked in the tower.[[85]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-p1627541851-85) Competition beyond its traditional rivals such as [Montgomery Ward](Montgomery_Ward "Montgomery Ward") arose from emerging retail giants including [Kmart](Kmart_(United_States) "Kmart (United States)"), <Kohl's>, and <Walmart>. As a result of a surplus of office space that emerged in the 1980s, the tower did not draw as many tenants as projected and so stood half-vacant for a decade.

#### Renovation and relocation

In February 1984, Sears announced that it would renovate the building to attract visitors to the lower floors.[[86]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n108282797-86)[[87]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n108282078-87) At the time, 6,500 Sears employees occupied more than half of the building,[[87]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n108282078-87)[[88]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n108282656-88) taking up the lowest 48 stories.[[88]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n108282656-88) The remainder of the tower was occupied by 5,500 employees from about 70 companies.[[87]](Willis_Tower#cite_note-n108282078-87) As part of the project, the main entrance was covered with a four-story glass dome, and the first four stories were converted into a shopping atrium. **111 West 57th Street**, also known as **Steinway Tower**, is a [supertall](Supertall "Supertall") residential skyscraper in the [Midtown Manhattan](Midtown_Manhattan "Midtown Manhattan") neighborhood of [New York City](New_York_City "New York City"). Developed by [JDS Development Group](JDS_Development_Group "JDS Development Group") and Property Markets Group, it is situated along [Billionaires' Row](Billionaires'_Row_(Manhattan) "Billionaires' Row (Manhattan)") on the north side of [57th Street](57th_Street_(Manhattan) "57th Street (Manhattan)") near [Sixth Avenue](Sixth_Avenue "Sixth Avenue"). The main portion of the building is an 84-story, 1,428-foot (435-meter) tower designed by [SHoP Architects](SHoP_Architects "SHoP Architects") and completed in 2021. Preserved at the base is the 16-story **Steinway Building** (also **Steinway Hall**), a former [Steinway & Sons](Steinway_%26_Sons "Steinway & Sons") store designed by [Warren and Wetmore](Warren_and_Wetmore "Warren and Wetmore") and completed in 1925, which originally carried the address 111 West 57th Street.

111 West 57th Street contains 60 [luxury condominiums](Luxury_apartment "Luxury apartment"): 14 in Steinway Hall and 46 in the tower. The residential tower has a glass [facade](Facade "Facade") with [piers](Pier_(architecture) "Pier (architecture)") made of [terracotta](Architectural_terracotta "Architectural terracotta"); its [pinnacle](Pinnacle "Pinnacle") contains [setbacks](Setback_(architecture) "Setback (architecture)") on the southern side. The tower is the fourth-[tallest building in the United States](List_of_tallest_buildings_in_the_United_States "List of tallest buildings in the United States") as of November 2022, as well as the thinnest skyscraper in the world with a [width-to-height ratio](Slenderness_ratio "Slenderness ratio") of about 1:24. Steinway Hall, a [New York City designated landmark](New_York_City_designated_landmark "New York City designated landmark"), contains a facade made mostly of brick, limestone, and terracotta. 111 West 57th Street contains numerous resident amenities, housed mostly in the building's base, as well as a large [rotunda](Rotunda_(architecture) "Rotunda (architecture)") within Steinway Hall that is also a designated city landmark.

The Steinway & Sons store at 111 West 57th Street was proposed in 1916 but was not completed for another nine years due to lawsuits and other delays. Steinway Hall served as a store, recital hall, and office building for almost nine decades, though it was unsuccessful as a [speculative development](Speculative_development "Speculative development"). Plans for a residential skyscraper on the site date to 2005, and JDS acquired the lots for the skyscraper between 2012 and 2013. Despite the tower's size, it was technically constructed as an addition to Steinway Hall. Construction on the tower began in 2014, and Steinway Hall was restored as part of the residential project. The development faced several challenges, including financing difficulties, lawsuits, and controversies over employment. The tower [topped out](Topping_out "Topping out") during April 2019 and was finished in 2021.

## Site

111 West 57th Street is in the [Midtown Manhattan](Midtown_Manhattan "Midtown Manhattan") neighborhood of [New York City](New_York_City "New York City"), just south of [Central Park](Central_Park "Central Park"), between [Sixth Avenue](Sixth_Avenue "Sixth Avenue") to the east and [Seventh Avenue](Seventh_Avenue_(Manhattan) "Seventh Avenue (Manhattan)") to the west. The building occupies the [land lots](Land_lot "Land lot") at 105–113 West 57th Street and contains [frontage](Frontage "Frontage") along [57th Street](57th_Street_(Manhattan) "57th Street (Manhattan)") to the south and 58th Street to the north.[[2]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NYCityMap-3) The rectangular site covers 20,621 square feet (1,915.8 m2), with a frontage of 106 feet (32 m) on 57th and 58th Streets, and a depth of 200.83 feet (61.21 m) between the two streets.[[3]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-ZoLa-4)

111 West 57th Street occupies the same [city block](City_block "City block") as the [Calvary Baptist Church](Calvary_Baptist_Church_(Manhattan) "Calvary Baptist Church (Manhattan)"), <One57>, and [Alwyn Court](Alwyn_Court "Alwyn Court") to the west, and abuts [The Quin](The_Quin "The Quin") immediately to the east. 111 West 57th Street is also near [Carnegie Hall](Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall"), [Carnegie Hall Tower](Carnegie_Hall_Tower "Carnegie Hall Tower"), and [Metropolitan Tower](Metropolitan_Tower_(Manhattan) "Metropolitan Tower (Manhattan)") one block west; [Parker New York](Parker_New_York "Parker New York"), [130 West 57th Street](130_West_57th_Street "130 West 57th Street"), and [140 West 57th Street](140_West_57th_Street "140 West 57th Street") across 57th Street to the south; and [Hampshire House](Hampshire_House "Hampshire House") and [Trump Parc](Trump_Parc "Trump Parc") across 58th Street to the north.[[2]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NYCityMap-3) The building stands across from the [57th Street station](57th_Street_station_(IND_Sixth_Avenue_Line) "57th Street station (IND Sixth Avenue Line)") of the [New York City Subway](New_York_City_Subway "New York City Subway")'s [M](M_(New_York_City_Subway_service) "M (New York City Subway service)") train.[[4]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-5)[[5]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-6) 111 West 57th Street is one of several major developments around 57th Street and Central Park that are collectively dubbed [Billionaires' Row](Billionaires'_Row_(Manhattan) "Billionaires' Row (Manhattan)") by the media. Other buildings along Billionaires' Row include [432 Park Avenue](432_Park_Avenue "432 Park Avenue") four blocks southeast, [220 Central Park South](220_Central_Park_South "220 Central Park South") one block northwest, [Central Park Tower](Central_Park_Tower "Central Park Tower") one block west, and the nearby One57.[[6]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-7)[[7]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-8)[[8]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-Vanity_Fair-9)

111 West 57th Street's base contains [Steinway Hall](Steinway_Hall "Steinway Hall"), a former store and recital hall for [Steinway & Sons](Steinway_%26_Sons "Steinway & Sons"). Steinway Hall was completed in 1925 by [Warren & Wetmore](Warren_and_Wetmore "Warren and Wetmore") and is a [New York City designated landmark](New_York_City_designated_landmark "New York City designated landmark").[[9]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-10)[[10]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NYCL_(2001)_p._4-11) Steinway Hall was part of an artistic hub developed around the two blocks of West 57th Street from Sixth Avenue west to [Broadway](Broadway_(Manhattan) "Broadway (Manhattan)") during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, following the opening of [Carnegie Hall](Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall") in 1891.[[11]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-12)[[12]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-13) The area contains several buildings constructed as residences for artists and musicians, such as 130 and 140 West 57th Street, the [Rodin Studios](Rodin_Studios "Rodin Studios"), and the [Osborne Apartments](Osborne_Apartments "Osborne Apartments"). In addition, the area contained the headquarters of organizations such as the [American Fine Arts Society](American_Fine_Arts_Society "American Fine Arts Society"), the [Lotos Club](Lotos_Club "Lotos Club"), and the [American Society of Civil Engineers](American_Society_of_Civil_Engineers "American Society of Civil Engineers").[[13]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-14)

## Architecture

111 West 57th Street, also known as Steinway Tower,[[14]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-AP_NEWS_2022-15) was developed by [Michael Stern](Michael_Stern_(real_estate_developer) "Michael Stern (real estate developer)")'s [JDS Development Group](JDS_Development_Group "JDS Development Group") and [Kevin P. Maloney](Kevin_P._Maloney "Kevin P. Maloney")'s Property Markets Group (PMG).[[1]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-The_Skyscraper_Center_2016-2)[[15]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-nyyimby20140102-16) [WSP USA](WSP_USA "WSP USA") was the structural engineer for the project, while [Jaros, Baum & Bolles](Jaros%2C_Baum_%26_Bolles "Jaros, Baum & Bolles") was the engineer in charge of mechanical, electrical, and plumbing.[[1]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-The_Skyscraper_Center_2016-2)

The building has two components. Warren and Wetmore's original Steinway Hall, at the base of the development, is topped by a 1,428 ft (435 m) tower designed by [SHoP Architects](SHoP_Architects "SHoP Architects"). According to documents filed by SHoP Architects principal Gregg Pasquarelli, the roof slab of the tower is 1,257 feet 6 inches (383.29 m) above ground level while the pinnacle is 1,423 feet 7 inches (433.91 m) above ground.[[16]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-Pasquarelli_p._165-17) The building contains 84 stories above ground level or 85 including the roof slab.[[1]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-The_Skyscraper_Center_2016-2)[[17]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-18)[[18]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-Pasquarelli_pp._185-186-19) The top story is numbered as floor 91, while floor numbers 5–7, 13, and 21–25 are skipped.[[18]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-Pasquarelli_pp._185-186-19)[[lower-alpha 1]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-marketing-levels-1) The tallest habitable story of the tower is 1,134 feet (346 m) above ground level.[[1]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-The_Skyscraper_Center_2016-2) There is also a sub-cellar and cellar, used primarily for utilities and storage.[[19]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-Pasquarelli_p._183-20)

### Form

The 16-story, "L"-shaped Steinway Hall fills most of the base, with frontages of 63 feet (19 m) along 57th Street and 100 feet (30 m) on 58th Street.[[20]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NYCL_(2001)_p._8-21)[[21]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-AB_p._71-22) The concert hall has a [setback](Setback_(architecture) "Setback (architecture)") above the 12th story on 57th Street, and setbacks above the 9th and 12th stories on 58th Street. The 16th story along 57th Street (marketed as floor 19[[lower-alpha 1]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-marketing-levels-1)) is also set back from all sides.[[10]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NYCL_(2001)_p._4-11) The roof of Steinway Hall contains a [campanile](Campanile "Campanile") with a pyramidal copper roof and lantern, similar to the [Mausoleum at Halicarnassus](Mausoleum_at_Halicarnassus "Mausoleum at Halicarnassus").[[22]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NY1930-23)[[23]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NYCL_(2001)_pp._9-10-24) [Christopher Gray](Christopher_Gray_(architectural_historian) "Christopher Gray (architectural historian)") of *[The New York Times](The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* described the campanile as having a "sculptural, even funerary, caste".[[24]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-25)

The residential tower atop Steinway Hall is one of the [tallest buildings in the United States](List_of_tallest_buildings_in_the_United_States "List of tallest buildings in the United States"), as well as the thinnest skyscraper in the world with a [width-to-height ratio](Slenderness_ratio "Slenderness ratio") of about 1:24.[[25]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-Marcus2015-26)[[26]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-27)[[27]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-28)[[lower-alpha 2]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-29) Due to its slenderness, the top stories sway several feet during high winds.[[14]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-AP_NEWS_2022-15) The building has been characterized as part of a new breed of New York City "[pencil towers](Pencil_tower "Pencil tower")".[[28]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-30) The tower's northern elevation rises directly up to the [pinnacle](Pinnacle "Pinnacle"), and the southern elevation contains several setbacks as the tower rises, thinning the tower's footprint on higher floors.[[8]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-Vanity_Fair-9)[[29]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-31)[[30]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-trd20150529-32)[[lower-alpha 3]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-33) The pinnacle's lighting pattern was commissioned by [L'Observatoire International](L'Observatoire_International "L'Observatoire International").[[1]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-The_Skyscraper_Center_2016-2)[[31]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-Hylton_2015-34) Because of the shape of the tower's pinnacle, 111 West 57th Street is nicknamed "Stairway to Heaven".[[15]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-nyyimby20140102-16)[[32]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-Mazzara_2016-35)

### Facade

#### Steinway Hall

On the first three stories of Steinway Hall's southern [elevation](Elevation_(architecture) "Elevation (architecture)"), facing 57th Street, the [facade](Facade "Facade") is made of [Indiana Limestone](Indiana_Limestone "Indiana Limestone") above a pink-granite [water table](Water_table_(architecture) "Water table (architecture)"). Two rectangular portals flank a large central arch there.[[21]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-AB_p._71-22)[[22]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NY1930-23)[[33]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NYCL_(2001)_p._9-36) The outer portals contain wooden pocket doors,[[33]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NYCL_(2001)_p._9-36)[[34]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-Pasquarelli_p._168-37) which are surrounded by moldings and topped with [entablatures](Entablature "Entablature").[[33]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NYCL_(2001)_p._9-36) The central opening is a display window that contains an entablature supported by [Ionic](Ionic_order "Ionic order") columns on either side, as well as a [lunette](Lunette "Lunette") above the entablature.[[35]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NYCL_(2013)_p._7-38) The lunette has a cement sculptural group by [Leo Lentelli](Leo_Lentelli "Leo Lentelli"), which contains a bas-relief of <Apollo>.[[21]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-AB_p._71-22)[[22]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NY1930-23)[[33]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NYCL_(2001)_p._9-36) Above the third story is a frieze with portraits of classical composers and pianists, as well as a central plaque with the name "Steinway".[[33]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NYCL_(2001)_p._9-36)

The northern elevation on 58th Street is clad with brick, limestone, and [terracotta](Architectural_terracotta "Architectural terracotta"). The lowest two floors are faced with [rusticated](Rustication_(architecture) "Rustication (architecture)") limestone blocks; the first floor has loading docks on either end of the 58th Street elevation.[[21]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-AB_p._71-22)[[33]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-NYCL_(2001)_p._9-36) One of the 58th Street loading docks led to a freight elevator for Steinway Hall's tenants, while the other led to a freight elevator used specifically by [Steinway & Sons](Steinway_%26_Sons "Steinway & Sons").[[21]](111_West_57th_Street#cite_note-AB_p._71-22)

Steinway Hall's upper stories are clad with brick. On 57th Street, there are three pairs of windows on each of the 4th through 12th stories. On 58th Street, there are five windows on each of the 3rd through 12th stories; there is a [balustrade](Baluster "Baluster") at the third story and a cornice atop the 9th story. 30 Hudson Yards is a supertall skyscraper in [Midtown Manhattan](Midtown_Manhattan "Midtown Manhattan")’s West Side, New York City. It’s strategically positioned near [Hell’s Kitchen](Hell's_Kitchen%2C_Manhattan "Hell's Kitchen, Manhattan"), Chelsea, and [NY Penn Station](New_York_Penn_Station "New York Penn Station"). As of November 2022, the building is the sixth-tallest in New York City and the eighth-tallest in the United States. It’s a key structure in the Hudson Yards Redevelopment Project, which aims to revitalize the [West Side Yard](West_Side_Yard "West Side Yard") of the [Metropolitan Transportation Authority.](Metropolitan_Transportation_Authority "Metropolitan Transportation Authority")

The skyscraper offers a unique feature: a triangular observation deck known as The Edge. Located on the 100th floor, The Edge includes a bar and event space on the adjacent 101st floor. The deck, at a height of 1,100 feet, is the world’s second-highest outdoor observation platform with transparent flooring, trailing only Madeira’s Skywalk.

30 Hudson Yards was previously the headquarters of <WarnerMedia>. Following a 2022 merger with Discovery, Inc., the new entity, [Warner Bros. Discovery](Warner_Bros._Discovery "Warner Bros. Discovery"), remains a tenant. The building also serves as the headquarters for [Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co](Kohlberg_Kravis_Roberts "Kohlberg Kravis Roberts")., an American global investment company.

## History

The groundbreaking ceremony took place on December 4, 2012. Early construction work focused on building a platform to cover much of the Eastern Rail Yard, for much of Phase 1 to sit upon and to allow the [Gateway Rail Tunnel project](Gateway_Tunnel "Gateway Tunnel") to pass underground with a clear path. The platform is rested on [caissons](Caisson_(engineering) "Caisson (engineering)") that are drilled underground into the solid [bedrock](Bedrock "Bedrock") known as [Manhattan schist](Manhattan_schist "Manhattan schist"). On December 12, 2013, it was announced that [Tutor Perini Building Corp.](Tutor_Perini "Tutor Perini") was awarded a US$510 million contract to build the platform.[[6]](30_Hudson_Yards#cite_note-6)

In 2013, [Time Warner](WarnerMedia "WarnerMedia") (later WarnerMedia, and now Warner Bros.
